headline: Massachusetts teacher survey finds student anxiety remains widespread
dek: A new UMass Amherst study finds 94% of surveyed public-school teachers see anxiety or depression as a problem for students, alongside concerns about poverty, housing and immigration status.
body: A new statewide survey of Massachusetts public-school teachers finds that student anxiety and depression remain a pervasive classroom concern, even as educators describe their relationships with students and classroom engagement in largely positive terms. The Annual Massachusetts Educator Survey, released Wednesday by the University of Massachusetts Amherst’s Center for Education Policy and UMass Amherst Poll, found that 94% of respondents considered anxiety and/or depression a problem or a big problem for their students. [UMass Amherst’s survey report](https://www.umass.edu/poll/about/reports/2026-10-annual-massachusetts-educator-survey) says the finding is part of a broader picture of unmet student and teacher needs across the Commonwealth.

The survey’s wording matters. It measured what teachers observe and believe about the problems facing students; it was not a clinical screening of children and does not establish how many students have a diagnosed mental-health condition. Within the responses, 48% called anxiety or depression a big problem and 46% called it a problem, while 6% said it was not a problem at all. That distinction allows the results to show the scale of teachers’ concern without turning their classroom observations into a medical count.

The same survey placed mental-health concerns alongside material and family pressures. Eighty-two percent of teachers identified poverty as a problem facing their students, while 74% cited homelessness, foster care or the loss of a caregiver. Seventy percent said immigration status had emerged as a student problem, and 56% identified drug or alcohol use as either a problem or a big problem. UMass says respondents could select more than one issue, so the percentages describe overlapping challenges rather than separate groups of children.

The findings are not a portrait of classrooms as uniformly disengaged or unsafe. UMass reported that 98% of teachers were somewhat or very satisfied with their professional relationships with students. Majorities said their students value learning, actively participate in class, treat one another with respect and treat teachers with respect. That contrast is important: educators can see serious needs outside the classroom while still reporting that students and teachers are building productive relationships inside it.

WBUR’s independent report on the survey illustrated the gap between those two realities through the account of Astrid Barrios, a Milford elementary-school teacher. Barrios told WBUR that one student regularly misses the beginning of a lesson because of anxiety and that other students have cried or shut down during classwork. Those experiences are one teacher’s account, not a statewide measurement, but they help explain how a problem recorded in survey percentages can affect attendance, concentration and the time available for instruction. [WBUR’s report](https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/10/14/massachusetts-public-school-teachers-student-mental-health) also quoted UMass researchers saying teachers often lack the time and training to respond to needs that enter the classroom.

Teachers’ proposed solutions point to staffing as well as individual support. Sixty-six percent selected more support staff, including counselors and paraprofessionals, among the top three school- or district-level changes that could help retain teachers. Better rules and procedures were selected by 60%, and 56% chose more supportive administrators. On contractual changes, 85% cited higher salaries and 60% cited better benefits. Those answers do not identify a single statewide remedy, but they show that respondents connect student needs with the working conditions that determine how much help a school can provide.

The survey also raises questions about who gets to shape the response. Only 19% of teachers said they were significantly included in developing their school improvement plan, and only 20% said the planning process works well. UMass researchers said the Annual Massachusetts Educator Survey was created to provide an ongoing view of educators’ experiences and to inform public discussion; this second wave therefore offers a baseline for comparing future findings rather than a final evaluation of any program.

UMass said it contacted 18,509 unique teacher email addresses between June 2 and Aug. 24 and received 1,179 completed surveys. The responses were weighted to match the state’s teacher population by gender identity, race and ethnicity, age, geographic area and grade level; the reported margin of error is 2.9%. The methodology improves the survey’s usefulness as a statewide estimate, but it does not eliminate the limits of asking teachers to report what they see. For Massachusetts districts, the immediate takeaway is a documented demand for more capacity around student well-being, while the funding, staffing and policy decisions needed to meet that demand remain unresolved.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: UMass survey finds widespread student anxiety in Massachusetts schools
seoDescription: A UMass Amherst survey found 94% of Massachusetts public-school teachers see student anxiety or depression as a problem, alongside poverty and housing concerns.
